extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, judges, and practitioners dealing with U.S. patent renewals, assignments, disclaimers, and licenses
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing surrender/reissue/renewal of patents, filing disclaimers, extensions, and the assignment vs license distinction under U.S. patent law (historic Act of 1836/1837 context). Useful for advising on transmission of patent interests and litigation/recording strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender and reissue for defective specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can lawfully receive a surrender of letters-patent for a defective specification, and issue new letters patent upon such surrender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new patent obtained on surrender for a defective specification may contain small amendments or corrections in the specification. The new letters-patent have been considered to operate, except as to suits for violations committed before the amendment, from the commencement of the original term; they relate back to the commencement of the original term and for many purposes should operate from that time. If a new patent issued on surrender is void for causes connected with public officers' acts, the original patent may remain in force until its term expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reissued/new patent on term and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A new patent issued on surrender is to be granted for the unexpired term only, by reference to the original grant, and may be granted for the whole remaining statutory term (e.g., fourteen years from original date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal effect of such a new patent is the same as if the patent had been specifically renewed for successive terms; it is not (generally) limited to run only from the date of the new letters. It is still a patent for the same invention and can include no new invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer for overbroad original claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is truly the patentee's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer may be filed in the patent office by the patentee, his administrator, executors, and assigns, whether of the whole or of a sectional interest in the patent; thereafter it is taken and considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest, and by those claiming by or under him subsequent to the record thereof. See also requirements under sections of Act of 1837 for when a disclaimer is to be filed and who should join.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent extension procedures and standard (board/commissioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are sometimes extended by special Acts of Congress; under Act of July 4, 1836, a board (Secretary of State, Commissioner of Patent Office, Solicitor of the Treasury) was to hear evidence and decide whether, with due regard to public interest, the patent term should be extended because the patentee failed to obtain reasonable remuneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commissioners, when satisfied that the patent ought to be renewed, certified the extension for a further term. By later statute, this power was vested solely in the Commissioner of Patents, who must refer the application to the principal examiner of the relevant class and decide upon substantially the same principles and rules formerly governing the board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities of assignment and recording requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent shall be assignable in law, either as to the whole interest, or any undivided part thereof, by any instrument in writing; such assignment and grants of exclusive rights must be recorded in the patent office within three months from execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording within three months is required to affect intermediate bona fide purchasers without notice; the assignee or grantee must pay prescribed recording fees. The statute prescribes recording but does not explicitly declare the assignment void if unrecorded; the provision is primarily for protection of purchasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes of interests required to be recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes of assignments/grants must be recorded: (1) an assignment of the whole patent; (2) an assignment of an undivided part of the whole patent; (3) a grant or conveyance of the exclusive right under any patent for any specified part or portion of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classes, if recorded within three months, will defeat intermediate bona fide purchasers; recording later will still be sufficient in other respects (e.g., to pass title between parties or for trial evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to record within three months (directory rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-month recording requirement is to be construed as directory rather than a condition precedent to validity; omission to record within three months does not necessarily render the assignment void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between patentee and assignee the assignment will be good despite non-recording; failing to record only affects priority against bona fide purchasers. Recording at any time before trial/hearing is sufficient for purposes of an action asserting title (i.e., admissible as evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording priority and protection of bona fide purchasers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the assignee fails to record within three months, a subsequent bona fide purchaser without notice during that period is preferred; if recording is made after three months but before a subsequent purchaser, the later purchaser may be postponed on ground of bad faith or constructive notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three-month period effectively gives the assignee that time to record without laches; the rule is aimed to protect purchasers acting in good faith and for valuable consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment vests indefeasible interest; patentee cannot defeat assignee by surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment vests in the assignee an interest in the patent indefeasible by act of the patentee; the patentee cannot, by a surrender of his patent, affect the rights of an assignee to whom he has previously granted the whole or part of the patent, without the assignee's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions authorizing surrender and reissue expressly save the rights of assignees. Strictly, an assignee should be a party to the surrender; but if not, previously made assignments are generally not vacated and assignees' interests remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee consent to surrender and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the assignee of a patent has consented to the surrender (even if not a party on the application record), the surrender enures to his benefit and becomes his act; he is thereby a proper party in infringement suits within the assigned territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee consenting to the surrender should be treated as having the rights and being a proper plaintiff; consent can transform the legal effect of the surrender as to the assignee's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of renewal/extension on assignees and grantees
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a statutory clause declaring 'the benefit of such renewal shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented to the extent of their respective interests therein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, it has been held that assignees under the original patent may not automatically acquire rights under an extended patent obtained pursuant to certain extension provisions unless such right is expressly conveyed to them by the patentee. Practical effect depends on the nature of the conveyance and statutory language; usage and prior recoveries under original patent may strengthen a claimant's right to an injunction after reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should file a disclaimer to obtain its benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disclaimer is to be filed under relevant statutory sections, an assignee of the whole patent is the proper party to file it; if the patent has been previously assigned in part, the disclaimer will not operate to the benefit of such an assignee in any suit by him unless he joined in the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure benefit in later litigation, partial assignees should join disclaimers affecting the patent or interest they claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and test between assignment and license
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment is a grant in writing of the whole or a part of the exclusive right vested in the patentee by the patent (and such grants must be recorded); a license grants the right to make, use, and sell the thing patented without transferring an exclusive interest in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether the instrument vests in the grantee the exclusive right to make and use the thing patented and to grant that right to others. If so, it is an assignment. If it merely grants a non-exclusive right to make/use/sell (even with numerical or territorial limits) it is a license and need not be recorded. Examples: grant to 'employ six persons' and vend matches was a license; an exclusive right in a district (even limited to a number of machines) that permits the grantee to grant rights to others is an assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment before patent issuance (future invention assignments)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be assigned for the patent before it is taken out so as to vest in the assignee the exclusive interest when the patent issues, but the application must be made and the specification duly sworn to by the inventor and the assignment recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalities must be observed (application by inventor, sworn specification, recording) for an assignment of a future patent to vest the assignee with the exclusive interest when the patent is later issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment by operation of law (bankruptcy) and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest in a patent passes to assignees in bankruptcy; if an invention has been perfected and an application made, the patent when issued will pass to the assignees. Whether a perfected invention for which no application had been made at the time of bankruptcy passes is a more difficult question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material in which the invention had been incorporated would pass, but the invention itself (which has not become a vested interest under the patent law until a proper application is made) may not. Courts have reasoned differently in English and U.S. contexts; due diligence in applying for patents affects the analysis.
